stem: Macroeconomic equilibrium in the AD/AS model is where

options.content: AD equals LRAS at every price level
options.rationale: LRAS shows potential output; equilibrium is with SRAS.

options.content: AD equals SRAS
options.rationale: Correct: the quantity of real output demanded equals the quantity supplied.

options.content: the price level equals the base year index
options.rationale: The base year index is not the equilibrium condition.

options.content: investment equals government spending
options.rationale: That is not the condition for AD/AS equilibrium.

explanation: Equilibrium is the price level and output at which AD equals SRAS.

stem: At a price level above the equilibrium, in the AD/AS model,

options.content: SRAS exceeds AD, and the price level tends to fall
options.rationale: Correct: excess supply puts downward pressure on prices.

options.content: AD exceeds SRAS, and the price level tends to rise
options.rationale: That describes a price level below equilibrium.

options.content: AD equals SRAS, and the price level is stable
options.rationale: That describes equilibrium itself.

options.content: LRAS shifts to the left until output falls
options.rationale: LRAS is not affected by the price level.

explanation: Above equilibrium, firms supply more than is demanded, so prices fall.

stem: A rightward shift of AD along an upward-sloping SRAS curve will cause

options.content: a rise in real output and a fall in the price level
options.rationale: That would result from a rightward shift of SRAS.

options.content: a fall in real output and a rise in the price level
options.rationale: That would result from a leftward shift of SRAS.

options.content: a fall in real output and a fall in the price level
options.rationale: That would result from a leftward shift of AD.

options.content: a rise in real output and a rise in the price level
options.rationale: Correct: the economy moves up along SRAS to a higher output and price level.

explanation: Demand-pull: AD shifts right, and the economy moves along SRAS to higher output and a higher price level.

stem: A sharp rise in the price of imported oil shifts SRAS to the left. The likely effects are

options.content: higher output and employment and a lower price level
options.rationale: That would be the effect of lower costs.

options.content: lower output and employment and a lower price level
options.rationale: A leftward AS shift raises prices.

options.content: lower output and employment and a higher price level
options.rationale: Correct: this is stagflation, from cost-push.

options.content: higher output and a higher price level
options.rationale: A fall in supply cannot raise output.

explanation: A leftward shift of SRAS along AD reduces output and raises the price level.

stem: At a price level of 75, AD is US\$5,350 million and SRAS is US\$4,900 million. Which statement is correct at this price level?

options.content: There is excess supply of 450 and the price level tends to fall
options.rationale: AD is larger than SRAS, so there is excess demand, not supply.

options.content: There is excess demand of 450 and the price level tends to rise
options.rationale: Correct: AD − SRAS = 5,350 − 4,900 = 450.

options.content: The economy is in equilibrium at this price level
options.rationale: Equilibrium needs AD to equal SRAS.

options.content: There is excess demand of 5,350 and the price level is stable
options.rationale: The excess is the difference between AD and SRAS, and it pushes the price up.

explanation: At 75, AD (5,350) exceeds SRAS (4,900) by 450: the price level rises.
hints: Subtract SRAS from AD at that price level.

stem: The economy is operating well below its potential output. An increase in government spending is most likely to cause

options.content: a rise in output and employment with only a small rise in prices
options.rationale: Correct: SRAS is shallow when there is spare capacity.

options.content: a large rise in prices and almost no change in output
options.rationale: That occurs near full capacity.

options.content: a fall in output because AD shifts left
options.rationale: Higher government spending shifts AD right.

options.content: a rise in potential output in the same year
options.rationale: Government spending shifts AD, not capacity, in the short run.

explanation: With spare capacity, firms can raise output without large cost increases, so most of the AD shift goes into output.
hints: How steep is SRAS when there is spare capacity?

stem: A rightward shift of SRAS caused by lower energy costs, with AD unchanged, will cause

options.content: a rise in the price level and a rise in real output
options.rationale: That would require AD to shift right.

options.content: a fall in the price level and a fall in real output
options.rationale: A rise in supply raises output.

options.content: no change in the price level because AD is fixed
options.rationale: The price level falls as SRAS shifts right.

options.content: a fall in the price level and a rise in real output
options.rationale: Correct: the economy moves down along AD to the right.

explanation: More is supplied at each price level, so equilibrium moves to a lower price level and higher output.
hints: Where does the new SRAS cross the old AD?

stem: A government states that a stimulus to AD will raise output and employment without inflation. Which fact would most weaken this claim?

options.content: The economy has large amounts of unemployed labour
options.rationale: Spare capacity supports the claim.

options.content: Firms have plenty of unused machinery
options.rationale: Idle machinery supports the claim.

options.content: The economy is already close to its potential output
options.rationale: Correct: SRAS is steep near full capacity, so mostly prices would rise.

options.content: The price level has been falling for several years
options.rationale: Falling prices suggest spare capacity, supporting the claim.

explanation: Near potential output, a rise in AD mostly raises prices (demand-pull) with little extra output.

stem:
Another fictional economy has the schedules below. AD then rises by US\$450 million at every price level. What is the new equilibrium real output, in US\$ million?

| Price level (index) | AD before (US\$ million) | SRAS (US\$ million) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 20 | 3,300 | 2,100 |
| 30 | 3,000 | 2,500 |
| 40 | 2,700 | 2,700 |
| 50 | 2,400 | 2,850 |
| 60 | 2,100 | 2,950 |
explanation: New AD: 3,750; 3,450; 3,150; 2,850; 2,550 at price levels 20 to 60. It equals SRAS at a price level of 50, where both are 2,850. (The original equilibrium output was 2,700 at a price level of 40.)
workedSolution: 1. New AD: 3,750; 3,450; 3,150; 2,850; 2,550 at price levels 20 to 60. It equals SRAS at a price level of 50, where both are 2,850. (The original equilibrium output was 2,700 at a price level of 40.)
hints: Add 450 to AD at each price level and find where it equals SRAS.

stem: After a rise in AD, equilibrium real output in a fictional economy moves from US\$6,400 million to US\$6,880 million. Calculate the percentage change in real output, to one decimal place.
In the same case the equilibrium price level rises from 140 to 154. Calculate the percentage change in the price level, to one decimal place.
hints: Compare the old price level with the new one.

stem: Each worker produces US\$15,000 of output a year, and employment moves with output. Calculate the rise in employment when equilibrium output rises from US\$3,800 million to US\$4,100 million.
explanation:
1. Employment before = 3,800,000,000 ÷ 15,000 = 253,333.
2. Employment after = 4,100,000,000 ÷ 15,000 = 273,333.
3. Rise = 20,000 workers (equivalently 300 million ÷ 15,000).
workedSolution:
1. 1. Employment before = 3,800,000,000 ÷ 15,000 = 253,333.
2. Employment after = 4,100,000,000 ÷ 15,000 = 273,333.
3. Rise = 20,000 workers (equivalently 300 million ÷ 15,000).
hints: Employment = output ÷ output per worker (watch the units: US\$ million to US\$).

| 100 | 5,600 | 6,050 |
| 110 | 5,300 | 6,150 |
explanation: New SRAS: 4,650; 5,250; 5,450; 5,600; 5,700. It equals AD (5,600) at a price level of 100, where output is 5,600. Output falls from 5,900 and the price level rises from 90 to 100.

stem: A leftward shift of SRAS causes both the price level and real output to rise.
explanation: False. A leftward shift of SRAS raises the price level but lowers real output (stagflation).

stem: A rightward shift of AD always increases real output by the same amount as the shift.
explanation: False. Because SRAS slopes upward, the price level rises and the increase in real output is smaller than the shift in AD; the closer to capacity, the smaller the rise in output.
hints: How steep is SRAS near capacity?

stem: State what is meant by macroeconomic equilibrium.

points.description: The position at which aggregate demand equals short-run aggregate supply.
Which determines the equilibrium price level and the level of real output.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Macroeconomic equilibrium is the position at which aggregate demand equals short-run aggregate supply, which determines the equilibrium price level and the level of real output.

explanation: One mark for AD = SRAS, one for price level and output.

stem: Explain the effect of a fall in consumer confidence on real output, the price level and employment.

points.description: Lower confidence reduces consumption, so AD shifts to the left.
The economy moves down along SRAS to a lower price level.
Real output falls.
Employment falls as firms need fewer workers.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lower confidence reduces consumption, so AD shifts to the left. The economy moves down along the SRAS curve to a lower price level and a lower level of real output. Firms need fewer workers, so employment falls.

explanation: AD left, price level lower, output lower, employment lower.
hints: Describe the shift first, then the move along SRAS.

stem: Analyse how a drought that reduces agricultural output could affect real output, prices and employment.

points.description: Food and raw materials become scarcer and dearer, raising firms' costs.
SRAS shifts to the left.
Real output falls and the price level rises (cost-push inflation).
Lower output means lower employment, so there is stagflation.
The effect may be temporary if harvests recover, as LRAS is unchanged.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The drought makes food and raw materials scarcer and more expensive, which raises firms' costs and shifts SRAS to the left. Real output falls and the price level rises, which is cost-push inflation. Lower output means lower employment, so the economy suffers stagflation. The effect may be temporary if harvests recover, since long-run capacity is not affected.

explanation: Costs up, SRAS left, output down and prices up, employment down, temporary.

stem:
**A fall in aggregate demand (illustrative data)**

A global recession reduces the demand for a fictional country's exports. The table shows AD before and after and the SRAS schedule. Employment moves with output; each worker produces US\$14,000 a year.

| Price level (index) | AD before (US\$ million) | AD after (US\$ million) | SRAS (US\$ million) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 12 | 7,400 | 6,650 | 5,400 |
| 22 | 7,000 | 6,250 | 6,250 |
| 32 | 6,600 | 5,850 | 6,600 |
| 42 | 6,200 | 5,450 | 6,800 |
| 52 | 5,800 | 5,050 | 6,950 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the equilibrium real output before the fall in AD, in US\$ million.
parts.explanation: Before: AD = SRAS = 6,600 at a price level of 32.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Before: AD = SRAS = 6,600 at a price level of 32.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the equilibrium real output after the fall in AD, in US\$ million.
parts.explanation: After: AD = SRAS = 6,250 at a price level of 22.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After: AD = SRAS = 6,250 at a price level of 22.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in real output (negative for a fall), to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the likely effect of the recession on the price level and employment.

points.description: The price level falls from 32 to 22 as AD shifts left along SRAS.
Output falls by 350, so firms need fewer workers.
Employment falls by about 25,000 (350 million ÷ 14,000).
Falling prices and rising unemployment indicate a demand-deficient slowdown.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: AD shifts to the left along the SRAS curve, so the price level falls from 32 to 22. Output falls by US\$350 million, so firms need fewer workers. Employment falls by about 25,000 (350 million divided by 14,000). Falling prices and rising unemployment are signs of weak demand.

explanation: Output 6,600 to 6,250 (−5.3%); price level 32 to 22; employment falls by about 25,000.

stem:
**An oil price shock (illustrative data)**

A sharp rise in the price of imported oil raises the cost of transport and production in a fictional country.

| Price level (index) | AD (US\$ million) | SRAS before (US\$ million) | SRAS after (US\$ million) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 105 | 4,950 | 3,900 | 3,450 |
| 115 | 4,700 | 4,400 | 3,950 |
| 125 | 4,450 | 4,450 | 4,000 |
| 135 | 4,200 | 4,650 | 4,200 |
| 145 | 3,950 | 4,780 | 4,330 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the new equilibrium price level after the shock.
parts.explanation: The new SRAS equals AD (4,200) at a price level of 135.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The new SRAS equals AD (4,200) at a price level of 135.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage change in real output (negative for a fall), to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the oil price rise is an example of cost-push inflation and stagflation.

points.description: Higher oil prices raise firms' costs of production, shifting SRAS to the left.
The price level rises (from 125 to 135): cost-push inflation.
Real output falls and unemployment rises while prices rise: stagflation.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Higher oil prices raise firms' costs of production, so SRAS shifts to the left. The price level rises from 125 to 135, which is cost-push inflation. At the same time real output falls and unemployment rises, so the economy suffers stagflation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the government should respond by increasing AD.

points.description: Raising AD would restore output and employment but make the price level rise further.
The shock is on the supply side, so demand policy is not a cure; it trades more inflation for output.
A judgement, for example that measures to cut costs or raise supply are better if the shock is lasting, while patience may be sufficient if it is temporary.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Raising AD would help to restore output and employment, but it would make the price level rise further, because the problem is on the supply side. If the oil price rise is lasting, measures that reduce costs or raise supply, such as improving energy efficiency, would be better; if the shock is temporary, it may be sensible to allow the economy to adjust.

explanation: New equilibrium price level 135; output −5.6%; cost-push and stagflation; demand policy trades prices for output.
hints: Find where AD equals the new SRAS.
Think about whether the shock is temporary.

stem: Evaluate the likely effects of a large increase in government spending on output, prices and employment in an economy.

points.description: Government spending is a component of AD, so a rise shifts AD to the right.
Output and employment rise as the economy moves along SRAS.
The price level also rises (demand-pull).
If there is much spare capacity, SRAS is shallow and most of the effect is on output and jobs.
If the economy is near potential output, SRAS is steep and most of the effect is on prices.
A multiplier effect may magnify the initial increase.
Imports may rise, reducing the effect on domestic output.
Financing: borrowing may raise interest rates and reduce private investment (crowding out), or add to debt.
If the spending is on infrastructure, LRAS may shift right over time, raising capacity.
Time lags: spending takes time to plan and carry out.
The effect depends on confidence and on whether the spending is efficient.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed, balanced analysis applied to the question, with evaluation and a supported judgement.
Some analysis and application; evaluation limited or judgement not supported.
Simple, undeveloped points with little application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: An increase in government spending shifts AD to the right, so output and employment rise as the economy moves along the SRAS curve, and the price level also rises (demand-pull). If there is much spare capacity, SRAS is shallow and most of the effect falls on output and jobs; if the economy is near potential output, SRAS is steep and most of the effect falls on prices. A multiplier effect may magnify the increase, but imports may rise and reduce the effect on domestic output. The spending has to be financed: borrowing may raise interest rates and reduce private investment (crowding out) or add to debt. If the spending is on infrastructure such as roads and power, LRAS may shift to the right over time, raising capacity and reducing the inflationary effect. There are also time lags, and the result depends on confidence and on how efficiently the money is spent. Overall, the increase is most beneficial when there is spare capacity and when the spending raises supply as well as demand.

explanation: Spare capacity, financing, multiplier, imports and supply effects weighed; judgement.
hints: Explain what spare capacity means for the slope of SRAS.
Consider the time lag and what else may change.
